<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line" lang="en">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">SingProbe Technical Report</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sing Team 
<br class="ltx_break">AI Security Lab
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Ant Group
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We present SingProbe, an open intrinsic guardrail framework for generation-time monitoring of large language models (LLMs). Intrinsic guardrails reuse hidden states already produced by the base model during autoregressive decoding, rather than relying on an independent model to repeatedly process generated text. While this route has been explored in industrial systems, the community lacks a broadly reusable open stack that combines cross-model guard adaptations, unified training methods, serving integrations, and systematic evaluation resources. SingProbe is designed to provide this missing layer.
SingProbe uses a lightweight probe to continuously produce query-intent, response-safety, and hallucination-risk signals during decoding. These signals support both response-level decisions and token-level risk localization. This report describes the full intrinsic-guardrail stack: training methods, serving integrations with SGLang and vLLM, and adapted guard models for 29 open-source base models across diverse families and scales. We also introduce SingStreamBench, a benchmark that measures whether streaming guardrails remain inactive on benign prefixes while promptly detecting emerging unsafe content.
Across evaluations of safety, streaming detection, hallucination detection, false-positive robustness, online monitoring, and runtime overhead, SingProbe provides performance competitive with, and in several settings stronger than, state-of-the-art standalone guardrails and specialized hallucination detectors, while adding less than 0.5% serving overhead in our implementation. Beyond passive monitoring, we show that intrinsic guard signals can guide constrained decoding and selectively activate medical-risk interventions in SingProbe-Med. By open-sourcing our infrastructure, training methods, and model adaptations, we aim to facilitate the broader adoption and deployment of intrinsic guardrails, as well as further research in this direction.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="id1" class="ltx_logical-block">
    
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><a href="https://github.com/inclusionAI/SingProbe" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href"><span class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-1.5pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2608.30703v2/github-logo.svg" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:16/16;" width="16" height="16"></object></span> https://github.com/inclusionAI/SingProbe</a></p>
<p id="p1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><a href="https://huggingface.co/collections/inclusionAI/singprobe" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href"><span class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-1.5pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2608.30703v2/hf-logo.svg" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:17/16;" width="17" height="16"></object></span> https://huggingface.co/collections/inclusionAI/singprobe</a></p>
</div>
  
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2608.30703v2/fig/tradeoff.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/197;" width="405" height="197" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Effectiveness–efficiency trade-off of guardrail models. Efficiency (x) is the extra inference latency of a guard over the base-model-only serving baseline. We use Ling-3.0-flash as the base model. A non-streaming guard is invoked once after the complete response has been generated, whereas a streaming guard is invoked at every generation step. Effectiveness (y-axis) is measured as the average of the guard’s Query F1 and Response F1 across the evaluated benchmarks. CC++/Kelp are our reproduced versions of two intrinsic guardrails <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cunningham et al., 2026</a>, <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, using the same model architecture and training data, with differences only in the training methodology.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this technical report, we propose SingProbe (<span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">S</span><span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">afety <span id="S1.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">in</span> <span id="S1.p1.1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">G</span>eneration <span id="S1.p1.1.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">Probe</span></span>), an open intrinsic guardrail framework for generation-time monitoring of large language models (LLMs). This report describes the complete SingProbe stack: its training methods, adapted guard models, serving integrations, and evaluation resources. Our objective is to make intrinsic guardrails a practical and deployable component, so that model developers and serving-system builders can train, deploy, and evaluate guardrails that operate within the generation pipeline.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">SingProbe is an intrinsic guardrail that reuses the hidden states that a base model already produces during autoregressive decoding, and applies a lightweight prediction module to emit risk signals. This differs from an external guardrail, which deploys a separate model to process the input or generated text independently <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2025</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Inan et al., 2023</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. The intrinsic route has already been explored in industrial systems, including Anthropic’s Constitutional Classifiers++ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cunningham et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and Alibaba Group’s Kelp/PlugGuard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. These efforts demonstrate the value of using internal representations for generation-time safety monitoring, but have primarily been developed for particular models or production settings. A broadly reusable open stack, including cross-model guard adaptations, unified training methods, standard serving integrations, and systematic evaluation resources, has not yet emerged. SingProbe is designed to provide this missing layer for the community.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">SingProbe converts base-model hidden states into a unified stream of guard signals. During generation, its lightweight probe continuously predicts query intent, response safety, and response hallucination risk. The resulting signals support two complementary uses: response-level decisions over completed trajectories and token-level localization of risks as they emerge. The training method is designed to learn useful streaming signals from commonly available coarse response-level supervision, enabling the same framework to support multiple monitoring tasks without requiring a separate text encoder.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Importantly, we make this framework deployable in common LLM serving systems. SingProbe is integrated with SGLang<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://github.com/jinzhen-lin/sglang/tree/token-probe-ling3-flash-main" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/jinzhen-lin/sglang/tree/token-probe-ling3-flash-main</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and vLLM<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://github.com/jinzhen-lin/vllm/tree/bailing-v3-token-probe" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/jinzhen-lin/vllm/tree/bailing-v3-token-probe</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, so decoding and guard scoring run in the same serving pipeline. This avoids repeatedly encoding generated text with an additional guard model and removes the need to coordinate a separate guardrail service. To support adoption across model families, we adapt and release SingProbe for 29 open-source base models spanning Ling 3.0, Qwen, Llama 3, Gemma 4, gpt-oss, GLM, Step, MiniMax, DeepSeek, and Hy. Each adaptation exposes the same interface for query intent, response safety, and hallucination monitoring.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate this stack across query-intent classification, response safety, streaming detection, hallucination detection, false-positive robustness, online monitoring, and runtime overhead. We also introduce <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SingStreamBench</span>, which evaluates a guardrail’s temporal behavior: it should remain inactive on benign prefixes and respond promptly when unsafe content emerges. Across these evaluations, SingProbe substantially reduces additional serving overhead while achieving performance competitive with, and in several settings stronger than, state-of-the-art standalone guardrails and specialized hallucination detectors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, SingProbe treats guard outputs as runtime control signals rather than only as classifier outputs. We study online monitoring under free autoregressive generation and SingProbe-guided constrained decoding. We further introduce <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SingProbe-Med</span>, which uses intrinsic signals to selectively activate medical-risk intervention on relevant suffixes instead of applying intervention continuously. These studies illustrate how the same monitoring interface can support downstream generation policies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, this report makes the following contributions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present SingProbe, an intrinsic guardrail framework that reuses LLM hidden states to continuously monitor query intent, response safety, and hallucination risk during generation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide an open intrinsic-guardrail stack comprising training methods, adapted models for 29 open-source base models, and serving integrations with SGLang and vLLM.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce SingStreamBench and systematically evaluate safety, hallucination, streaming behavior, false positives, online monitoring, and runtime overhead.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate that intrinsic guard signals can support generation-time control, including constrained decoding and selective medical-risk intervention.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Methodology</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Formulation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math> denote an autoregressive LLM with <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> layers. Given a token sequence <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})</annotation></semantics></math>, the model produces a hidden state <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> for token <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> at layer <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>. Rather than introducing an additional text encoder, SingProbe directly takes the concatenated hidden states from a selected subset of layers <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>⊆</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}</annotation></semantics></math> as its input. Abstracting the fusion of the selected hidden states into a lightweight prediction head <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, the token-level output is defined as</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{t}=g_{\theta}\!\left(\left\{\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\right\}_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}}\right)=\left[\mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{query}}_{t},\,s^{\mathrm{unsafe}}_{t},\,s^{\mathrm{hallu}}_{t}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{\mu+1+1}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mrow><mo>{</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>query</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>unsafe</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>hallu</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{t}=g_{\theta}\!\left(\left\{\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\right\}_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}}\right)=\left[\mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{query}}_{t},\,s^{\mathrm{unsafe}}_{t},\,s^{\mathrm{hallu}}_{t}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{\mu+1+1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{query}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>query</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>μ</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{query}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mu}</annotation></semantics></math> contains <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> fine-grained query-intent scores, while <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{\mathrm{unsafe}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>unsafe</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{\mathrm{unsafe}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{\mathrm{hallu}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>hallu</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{\mathrm{hallu}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> respectively represent the response-unsafety and hallucination scores. All scores are produced at every token position. Because each selected hidden state depends only on the current prefix <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{\leq t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{\leq t}</annotation></semantics></math>, SingProbe provides causally updated predictions throughout generation, enabling token-level streaming detection without an additional encoding pass. We treat these outputs as logits and apply task-specific normalization when probabilities or decisions are required.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Query Intent Classification.</span> Following SingGuard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Group, 2026</a>)</cite>, we organize query intents into eight categories and use the first eight outputs of SingProbe as their class scores: <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(A)</span> Sexual Content Risk, <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(B)</span> Real-World Crimes &amp; Public Safety, <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(C)</span> Unethical Behavior, <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(D)</span> Cybersecurity &amp; Information Manipulation, <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(E)</span> Agent Safety, <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(F)</span> Politically Sensitive Content, <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(G)</span> Animal Abuse, and <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(H)</span> Safe. The first seven categories cover different types of potentially harmful intent, while Safe indicates that the query does not match any active risk category. A higher class score indicates stronger evidence for the corresponding intent category.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Response Safety and Hallucination Classification.</span> The other output scores track risks in the generated response. The response-unsafety score measures the safety risk of the response prefix generated up to the current token, while the hallucination score estimates the likelihood that the generated content contains hallucinations. Higher values indicate that the response is more likely to be unsafe or contain hallucinations, respectively. Both scores are updated throughout decoding, providing streaming risk signals that can support early intervention.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2608.30703v2/overview.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/245;" width="452" height="245" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>The overview of SingProbe. <span id="S2.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top:</span> SingProbe replaces the conventional external guard paradigm with an intrinsic guard that operates alongside autoregressive decoding. <span id="S2.F2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bottom right:</span> It directly consumes concatenated hidden states from selected base-model layers and produces token-level signals for query intent, response safety, and hallucination risk. <span id="S2.F2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bottom left:</span> These streaming signals support applications including unsafe content detection, constrained decoding, and generation-time intervention.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Training Objectives</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We could jointly train SingProbe for any query- or response-classification task. In our implementation, we train SingProbe on query-intent classification, response-safety classification, and response-hallucination detection. The three objectives are combined as</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=w_{q}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{query}}+w_{s}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{safety}}+w_{h}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{hallu}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>total</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>query</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>safety</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>hallu</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=w_{q}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{query}}+w_{s}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{safety}}+w_{h}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{hallu}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{h}</annotation></semantics></math> weight the query-intent, response-safety, and response-hallucination objectives, respectively. Rather than keeping these weights fixed, we update them based on exponential moving averages (EMAs) of the corresponding losses, assigning larger weights to tasks with higher recent losses while retaining their configured base weights. Concretely, let <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\tau}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\tau}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the loss of task <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in\{q,s,h\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in\{q,s,h\}</annotation></semantics></math> at step <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\tau}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\tau}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> its EMA updated with smoothing coefficient <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\tau}^{(t)}=\alpha\,\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\tau}^{(t-1)}+(1-\alpha)\,\mathcal{L}_{\tau}^{(t)},\qquad\tau\in\{q,s,h\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\tau}^{(t)}=\alpha\,\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\tau}^{(t-1)}+(1-\alpha)\,\mathcal{L}_{\tau}^{(t)},\qquad\tau\in\{q,s,h\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The per-step weight is then obtained by scaling the base weight <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\tau}^{\mathrm{base}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>τ</mi><mi>base</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\tau}^{\mathrm{base}}</annotation></semantics></math> with the ratio of the task’s EMA loss to the mean of those EMAs, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\mathcal{L}}^{(t)}=\text{Mean}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\tau}^{(t)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Mean</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\mathcal{L}}^{(t)}=\text{Mean}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\tau}^{(t)})</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\tau}^{(t)}=w_{\tau}^{\mathrm{base}}\,\frac{\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\tau}^{(t)}}{\bar{\mathcal{L}}^{(t)}}\ ,\qquad\tau\in\{q,s,h\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>τ</mi><mi>base</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><msup><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\tau}^{(t)}=w_{\tau}^{\mathrm{base}}\,\frac{\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\tau}^{(t)}}{\bar{\mathcal{L}}^{(t)}}\ ,\qquad\tau\in\{q,s,h\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Dividing by <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\mathcal{L}}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\mathcal{L}}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> reweights each task in proportion to its recent difficulty (larger recent loss <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇒</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> larger weight), while the three ratios average to 1, so the overall loss magnitude is preserved. We set <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha{=}0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha{=}0.9</annotation></semantics></math> and guard the denominator against zero with a small floor of <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-9}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-9}</annotation></semantics></math>. This allows training to focus on the currently more difficult objectives as optimization progresses. The details of the above objectives are introduced as follows.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.1 </span>Query-Intent Objective</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The query-intent objective applies binary cross-entropy (BCE) independently to the seven risk categories, allowing multiple risks to coexist, and to the Safe category, which is mutually exclusive with all risk categories. In addition to this label-level constraint, we introduce a soft mutual-exclusion loss that penalizes simultaneously high predictions for Safe and the most probable risk category. This encourages a clear separation between safe and risky queries without restricting co-occurrence among different risk types. The query-intent loss is defined as</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="S2.E5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S2.E5X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{query}}={}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>query</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{query}}={}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{b}\!\Biggl[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{b}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{V}_{b}}\Biggl(\frac{1}{\mu-1}\sum_{k=0}^{\mu-2}\mathrm{BCE}(\ell_{b,t,k},y_{b,t,k})+\lambda_{\mathrm{safe}}\mathrm{BCE}(\ell_{b,t,\mu-1},y_{b,t,\mu-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub><mo maxsize="2.600em" minsize="2.600em">[</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo></mstyle><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo maxsize="2.600em" minsize="2.600em">(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo></mstyle><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>BCE</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>λ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>safe</mi></msub><mi>BCE</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{b}\!\Biggl[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{b}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{V}_{b}}\Biggl(\frac{1}{\mu-1}\sum_{k=0}^{\mu-2}\mathrm{BCE}(\ell_{b,t,k},y_{b,t,k})+\lambda_{\mathrm{safe}}\mathrm{BCE}(\ell_{b,t,\mu-1},y_{b,t,\mu-1})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.E5Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{mutex}}\,\sigma(\ell_{b,t,\mu-1})\max_{0\leq k\leq\mu-2}\sigma(\ell_{b,t,k})\Biggr)\Biggr]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>λ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>mutex</mi></msub><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>max</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo maxsize="2.600em" minsize="2.600em">)</mo><mo maxsize="2.600em" minsize="2.600em">]</mo><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{mutex}}\,\sigma(\ell_{b,t,\mu-1})\max_{0\leq k\leq\mu-2}\sigma(\ell_{b,t,k})\Biggr)\Biggr].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the valid supervised positions in sample <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>; <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{b,t,k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{b,t,k}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{b,t,k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{b,t,k}</annotation></semantics></math> are the logit and label for category <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> at position <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>; <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is the sigmoid function; and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\mathrm{safe}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>safe</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\mathrm{safe}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\mathrm{mutex}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>mutex</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\mathrm{mutex}}</annotation></semantics></math> control the Safe loss and mutual-exclusion penalty, respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.2 </span>Response Safety and Hallucination Objectives</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Streaming response detection requires learning from every generation prefix, yet available safety and hallucination datasets typically provide only response-level labels rather than fine-grained token-level supervision. Qwen3Guard-Stream <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2025</a>)</cite> addresses this problem by generating multiple rollouts from each token prefix and estimating its risk from the proportion of unsafe continuations, followed by LLM-based verification. Although this procedure produces fine-grained boundary labels, repeatedly generating and judging multiple continuations for every prefix incurs substantial annotation cost. Constitutional Classifier++ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cunningham et al., 2026</a>)</cite> instead avoids explicit token-level annotation through a softmax-weighted objective that concentrates supervision on tokens with high predicted harmfulness. However, because the weights are determined directly by the current logits, this strategy can be sensitive to poorly calibrated predictions at initialization: spuriously high-scoring tokens may receive disproportionate weights and amplify early training noise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Based on the above understanding, we therefore adopt an adaptive confidence-weighted aggregator that activates confidence weighting only when token predictions are sufficiently differentiated and otherwise falls back to uniform averaging. The response-safety and response-hallucination objectives are both trained with token-level BCE under this aggregator. Let <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\in\mathcal{R}=\{\mathrm{safety},\mathrm{hallu}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>safety</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>hallu</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\in\mathcal{R}=\{\mathrm{safety},\mathrm{hallu}\}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the task and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> its output dimension, where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\mathrm{safety}}=\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>safety</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\mathrm{safety}}=\mu</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\mathrm{hallu}}=\mu+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>hallu</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\mathrm{hallu}}=\mu+1</annotation></semantics></math>. The corresponding objective is defined as</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="S2.E6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S2.E6X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E6X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{r}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E6X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{b}\!\left[\sum_{t\in\mathcal{V}_{b}}\alpha^{(r)}_{b,t}\,\mathrm{BCE}(\ell_{b,t,c_{r}},y_{b,t,c_{r}})\right]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></munder></mstyle><mrow><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>BCE</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{b}\!\left[\sum_{t\in\mathcal{V}_{b}}\alpha^{(r)}_{b,t}\,\mathrm{BCE}(\ell_{b,t,c_{r}},y_{b,t,c_{r}})\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.E6Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E6Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\alpha^{(r)}_{b,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\alpha^{(r)}_{b,t}</annotation></semantics></math></td>

p^{(r)}_{b,t}=\sigma(\ell_{b,t,c_{r}})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>softmax</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\operatorname{softmax}_{t\in\mathcal{V}_{b}}\!\left(\frac{\beta_{r}\,p^{(r)}_{b,t}}{T}\right),\qquad\beta_{r}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{std}_{(b,t)\in\mathcal{V}}(p^{(r)}_{b,t})}{\tau},0,1\right),\quad p^{(r)}_{b,t}=\sigma(\ell_{b,t,c_{r}}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p^{(r)}_{b,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p^{(r)}_{b,t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the predicted risk probability and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{(r)}_{b,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha^{(r)}_{b,t}</annotation></semantics></math> is its normalized token weight. The factor <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> controls the strength of confidence weighting according to the dispersion of valid predictions. When predictions are insufficiently differentiated, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> approaches zero and the aggregator reduces to uniform averaging, preventing early training noise from being amplified. Once the predictions become sufficiently differentiated, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> increases and the softmax assigns greater weight to tokens with higher predicted risk—unsafety for response safety and hallucination probability for hallucination detection. <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is the weighting temperature, and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> controls the sensitivity of the adaptive factor.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">This confidence weighting has complementary effects on negative and positive samples. For safe or non-hallucinated responses, high-risk tokens correspond to potential false positives; emphasizing their losses directly suppresses spurious risk peaks. For unsafe or hallucinated responses, tokens in a benign prefix typically receive lower risk scores and are therefore downweighted relative to the later risk-bearing tokens. This prevents the response-level positive label from incorrectly pushing every prefix toward the risky class. Moreover, because the weights are normalized separately within each sample, a benign prefix receives a larger relative weight in a negative response, where no genuinely risky continuation dominates the weighting distribution, than in a positive response containing later high-risk tokens. Consequently, similar benign prefixes receive stronger supervision toward the safe or non-hallucinated class from negative samples while remaining largely unaffected by the coarse positive labels of unsafe or hallucinated samples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">All objectives are computed only at response positions with valid labels. Because token weights are normalized within each sample, longer responses do not dominate training.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Training Dataset Construction</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training SingProbe requires stable supervision for learning safety- and factuality-related decision boundaries in the hidden-state space of the backbone LLM. We therefore construct a unified corpus for three tasks: <em id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">query intent classification</em>, <em id="S2.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">response safety classification</em>, and <em id="S2.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">response hallucination detection</em>.
The final corpus covers harmful prompts, benign but sensitive prompts, harmful responses, safe refusals, and helpful safe completions. Each example follows a unified format containing a user query, optional dialogue context, and an optional assistant response. Query-side and response-side labels are maintained separately, allowing the same data source to support prompt screening, response monitoring, and joint query–response classification. The corpus is constructed through open-source data curation, policy-grounded synthesis, and multi-stage quality control.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Open-Source Data Curation.</span>
We use only the official training splits of publicly available safety benchmarks and training datasets. Because different sources adopt different annotation protocols, risk granularities, and decision thresholds, directly merging their labels would introduce inconsistent supervision. We therefore normalize all safety examples under the fine-grained risk taxonomy introduced in this work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For datasets with existing annotations, the original labels are first mapped to our taxonomy using predefined category correspondences and then independently verified by an LLM judge under our safety definitions. Samples with consistent labels are retained, whereas ambiguous cases, including potential safe/unsafe polarity flips, are moved to an unlabeled hard-case pool. For unlabeled data and hard cases, multiple open-source LLMs, including Qwen3.5-397B-A17B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026a</a>)</cite> and Kimi-K2.6 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moonshot AI, 2026</a>)</cite>, independently annotate each example. We combine self-consistency across repeated predictions from the same model with agreement across different models. Each accepted sample must pass both a binary safe/unsafe consistency check and a fine-grained category check. Samples failing the binary check are discarded, while samples with unresolved category disagreement are retained only after targeted review.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For hallucination supervision, we additionally incorporate the training splits of public factuality and hallucination datasets, labeling correct answers and honest refusals as <em id="S2.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">non-hallucinated</em> and incorrect, fabricated, or unsupported answers as <em id="S2.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">hallucinated</em>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Policy-Grounded Safety Data Synthesis.</span>
Open-source safety data are typically long-tailed and provide limited coverage of emerging or low-frequency risks. We therefore supplement them with policy-grounded synthetic data. For each risk category, an internally red-teamed jailbreak model generates harmful prompts, while an aligned model produces topically similar but benign counterparts. These contrastive pairs share surface vocabulary but differ in their underlying intent, discouraging SingProbe from relying on lexical shortcuts for the safety task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We further generate multiple responses for each prompt. Unsafe prompts are paired with both harmful responses and policy-compliant refusals or safe alternatives, while benign prompts are paired with helpful and compliant responses. This construction prevents response safety from being inferred directly from the prompt label and encourages SingProbe to track the evolving response representation. We additionally synthesize multi-category and multilingual examples to improve coverage of compositional and cross-lingual risks. All synthetic samples are independently re-evaluated by an LLM that is not involved in generation, and samples whose predicted labels disagree with the intended labels are removed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Quality Control and Training Supervision.</span>
We remove duplicate and near-duplicate examples, balance safe and unsafe instances across major risk categories, and retain high-confidence boundary cases that distinguish harmful intent from benign discussions of sensitive topics. During training, the curated examples are processed by the backbone LLM to obtain the hidden states used by SingProbe. Query labels are aligned with representations at the query boundary, while response-safety and hallucination labels supervise representations produced along the response trajectory. This formulation enables SingProbe to jointly monitor user intent, response safety, and factual reliability without requiring an additional text encoder or a separately deployed guardrail model.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>SingStreamBench: Benchmarking Streaming Safety Detection</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Motivation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing safety benchmarks are primarily designed for post-hoc classification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2023</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazeika et al., 2024</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghosh et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and provide only a single response-level label. Such labels indicate whether a completed response is unsafe, but do not reveal when unsafe content first emerges during generation. Consequently, they cannot adequately evaluate whether a streaming guardrail remains silent on benign prefixes, detects the actual onset of harmful content, or intervenes with minimal delay.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">FineHarm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> takes an important step toward fine-grained evaluation by providing token-level harmfulness annotations. Its annotations are constructed heuristically: responses are first labeled at the sentence level using an LLM, after which content words in harmful sentences are marked as harmful and their labels are mapped to the corresponding tokens. However, our manual inspection reveals substantial noise in these fine-grained labels. More fundamentally, harmfulness is often expressed compositionally and depends on surrounding context, making it difficult to assign a stable safety label to an individual token in isolation. These issues limit the reliability of token-level labels as ground truth for evaluating the precise onset of unsafe content.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Even when fine-grained labels can be obtained, the composition of existing safety datasets introduces another limitation. Most unsafe responses begin producing harmful content near the start of the response, resulting in a strong positional bias and few examples containing a substantial safe prefix before the unsafe segment. A classifier may therefore appear effective by reacting to the unsafe query or early lexical cues, without demonstrating that it can remain inactive throughout benign content and trigger only when harmful content actually appears.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Based on these observations, we construct a manually verified fine-grained benchmark, <span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SingStreamBench</span>, and a larger-scale version, <span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SingStreamBench-Full</span>, to evaluate both the accuracy and timeliness of streaming safety detection. Instead of assigning intrinsic labels to isolated tokens, we segment each response into sentences and annotate its cumulative sentence-level prefixes to identify a semantically meaningful unsafe onset boundary. We further construct controlled safe-to-unsafe transitions and fully safe counterexamples, organized into six tiers that vary the complexity and safety composition of both queries and response prefixes. This design enables explicit evaluation of whether a guardrail remains silent before risk emerges, detects the true unsafe segment promptly, and avoids relying on spurious query or positional cues.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Benchmark Design</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each benchmark sample consists of a query <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{q}</annotation></semantics></math> and a response <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐫</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}</annotation></semantics></math> that can be conceptually decomposed as</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{safe}}\oplus\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{target}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>safe</mi></msup><mo>⊕</mo><msup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>target</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{safe}}\oplus\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{target}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{safe}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>safe</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{safe}}</annotation></semantics></math> is an optional safe prefix and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{target}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>target</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{target}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the continuation whose safety status determines the response label. The central evaluation target is the transition around the beginning of <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{target}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>target</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{target}}</annotation></semantics></math>: a reliable streaming guardrail should remain silent throughout the safe prefix and react promptly once unsafe content emerges. For fully safe responses, it should remain silent throughout generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We organize the benchmark into six tiers, as summarized in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Benchmark Design ‣ 3 SingStreamBench: Benchmarking Streaming Safety Detection ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. The tiers progressively test spurious associations with the query or safe prefix and robustness to increasingly complex contexts.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Tiered construction of SingStreamBench.</figcaption>

<th id="S3.T1.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt">
<span id="S3.T1.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:69.0pt;">
<span id="S3.T1.2.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.T1.2.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Query</span></span>

</span></td></tr>
