</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="S3.T1.2.7.4.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:148.3pt;">
<span id="S3.T1.2.7.4.1.1" class="ltx_p">Jointly test complex query context and a substantial safe response prefix before unsafe content appears.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Tiers 1 and 2 primarily diagnose false associations. Tier 1 tests whether an unsafe query alone causes the response stream to be flagged even when the model safely refuses, while Tier 2 tests whether a safe prefix itself induces false alarms when followed by a safe continuation. Tiers 3–5 introduce more complex contexts. Tier 3 inserts background knowledge or a disclaimer before the original unsafe response; Tier 4 prepends query-related background text to the query; and Tier 5 combines one unsafe question with multiple safe questions, producing a multi-question context in which safe content precedes the unsafe segment. Together, these tiers distinguish genuine localization of response risk from shortcuts based on query harmfulness, response position, or superficial lexical cues.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Construction Pipeline</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The benchmark is constructed through the following four-stage pipeline.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Seed sampling and verification.</span> We sample query–response pairs from existing safety datasets and re-evaluate whether each response-level label is correct. Three judge models, Qwen3-235B-A22B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, GLM-5.2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and Kimi-K2.6 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moonshot AI, 2026</a>)</cite>, independently verify each sample, and only samples unanimously accepted by all three models are retained. This step removes mislabeled and ambiguous seed responses.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tiered data augmentation.</span> Starting from a verified unsafe query–response pair, we construct four types of augmented samples. For Tier 1, a safe refusal is generated for the unsafe query. For Tier 3, the model generates safe background information or a disclaimer that is prepended to the original unsafe response. For Tier 4, query-related background text is generated and prepended to the original query. For Tier 5, one unsafe question is combined with one to three sampled safe questions using a multi-question template such as “Please answer the following questions: 1. …; 2. …”. For each generation operation, one of the three models above is selected at random to increase stylistic and model diversity.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sentence-boundary prefix annotation.</span> Each response is first segmented into sentences <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math>. We then construct cumulative prefixes <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{j}=\mathbf{u}_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbf{u}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>⊕</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>⊕</mo><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{j}=\mathbf{u}_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbf{u}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> and use Kimi-K2.6 to assign a Safe or Unsafe label to each prefix <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, rather than labeling each sentence in isolation. For an unsafe response, annotation proceeds sequentially and stops once the first unsafe prefix is identified; the starting position of its newly added sentence is recorded as <span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Unsafe_Start_Index</span>. All preceding prefixes are treated as safe. For a safe response, every sentence-level prefix is verified as safe. This procedure directly identifies the safe-prefix boundary required for streaming evaluation while avoiding token-level semantic ambiguity.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Safe-continuation augmentation.</span> To construct Tier 2, we sample examples with a non-empty safe prefix and ask a model to continue generation safely from the corresponding query and prefix. The resulting fully safe responses test whether a guardrail can remain inactive after observing prefixes that may otherwise also occur before unsafe continuations.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Dataset Variants and Statistics</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The construction pipeline produces two benchmark variants. <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SingStreamBench</span> is the high-quality core benchmark containing 210 samples that have undergone manual verification. <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SingStreamBench-Full</span> is the larger-scale variant containing 2,428 constructed samples, providing broader coverage across tiers and safety scenarios. The original queries and responses are partly from BeaverTails <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, PKU-SafeRLHF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, WildGuard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, XSTest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Röttger et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and expguard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choi et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. The manually verified core set supports reliable comparison of streaming detection accuracy and latency, while the full set enables evaluation at a larger scale.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Evaluation</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Settings</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Safety Guard Baselines.</span> We compare SingProbe against two proprietary LLMs and 12 open-source guardrail configurations. The proprietary baselines are Gemini 3 Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google, 2025</a>)</cite> and GPT-5.1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>)</cite>. The open-source baselines include YuFeng-XGuard-Reason-0.6B/8B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, Llama Guard 3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Inan et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, WildGuard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, GraniteGuardian <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Research, 2024</a>)</cite>, ShieldGemma-9B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng and others, 2024</a>)</cite>, and Qwen3Guard series <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. For Qwen3Guard, we evaluate both loose and strict modes, which respectively treat the Controversial label as safe and unsafe. Some of the baselines’ evaluation results are from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Group (2026)</a></cite>. We additionally implement three intrinsic-guard baselines: <em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Vanilla</em>, which uses standard uniformly averaged BCE; <em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">CC++</em>, which reproduces Anthropic’s Constitutional Classifier++ objective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cunningham et al., 2026</a>)</cite>; and <em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Kelp</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. To ensure a fair comparison, all three baselines use the same training datasets, Ling-3.0-flash base model, and model architecture as SingProbe. Because these methods are designed specifically for response safety, we compare them only on response-safety evaluations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hallucination Detection Baselines.</span> We compare SingProbe with four representative hidden-state-based hallucination detectors: DRIFT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhatnagar et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, HaMI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and SAPLMA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Azaria and Mitchell, 2023</a>)</cite>. These methods cover lightweight probing, adaptive token selection, and training-free NTK-based scoring. For SAPLMA, we evaluate both the raw-input and response-formatted variants, denoted SAPLMA-raw and SAPLMA-response, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implementation Details of SingProbe.</span> In our experiments, we implement a unified SingProbe architecture based on a query-residual multi-head attention (MHA) block. Specifically, the block computes queries <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math>, keys <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, and values <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> and produces the attention output <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>O</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O</annotation></semantics></math>, and finally outputs <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Norm}(Q+O)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Norm</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Norm}(Q+O)</annotation></semantics></math>, followed by a linear classifier that produces the guardrail scores. As the default setting, we use hidden states from three layers of the base model as input to SingProbe, with the layers evenly selected from the shallow, middle, and deep portions of the model. Unless otherwise stated, the main-text experiments use Ling-3.0-tiny-singprobe and Ling-3.0-flash-singprobe. We additionally extend SingProbe to 29 open-source base models spanning diverse model families, parameter scales, and architectures; the additional model-wise results are provided in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Evaluation of Adapted SingProbe Models ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">

</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Query Classification Evaluation ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reports the query-intent classification results across six benchmarks, including Aegis2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghosh et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, XGuard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, OpenAI Moderation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Markov et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, XSTest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Röttger et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, HarmBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazeika et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and ExpGuard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choi et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. For each sample, we feed the query to the base model and let it generate a response with a maximum length of 512. SingProbe produces query-intent scores at every token position in the generated response. We then average these scores across response positions and use the resulting eight-dimensional score vector as the final query-intent prediction. The best configuration, SingProbe with Ling-3.0-flash, achieves an average F1 of 0.8674, ranking closely behind YuFeng-XGuard-Reason-8B (0.8714) and GPT-5.1 (0.8683). It also outperforms all evaluated Qwen3Guard configurations, whose best average F1 is 0.8602, as well as other widely used guardrails such as WildGuard and Llama Guard 3. These results show that an intrinsic lightweight head can provide query-safety classification performance comparable to substantially larger standalone guardrail models and frontier proprietary LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The results further demonstrate consistent benefits from scaling the base model. Replacing Ling-3.0-tiny with Ling-3.0-flash improves the average F1 of SingProbe from 0.8561 to 0.8674, indicating that stronger base-model hidden states provide richer query-safety signals for the lightweight head. SingProbe is competitive with the strongest standalone guardrails across the six benchmarks and achieves the best F1 on ExpGuardTest (0.8825), suggesting that the base model’s hidden states already contain strong query-safety signals that can be effectively extracted by a lightweight temporal head.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Response Safety Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate response safety from three complementary dimensions: <em id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">response-level classification</em>, which measures whether a guardrail correctly identifies the overall safety of a completed response; <em id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">streaming detection</em>, which evaluates both response-level discrimination and token-level risk localization throughout generation; and <em id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">false-positive robustness</em>, which measures whether the guardrail remains silent on nominally benign queries and freely generated responses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Response-level Classification.</span> We first evaluate response safety under teacher forcing by feeding each query together with its labeled response. We evaluate 8 benchmarks including BeaverTails <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, PKU-SafeRLHF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Aegis2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghosh et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, WildGuard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, XGuard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, HarmBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazeika et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, XSTest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Röttger et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and ExpGuard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choi et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. SingProbe produces a response-safety score at every response position, and we use the maximum score over the entire response as the final response-level risk score. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Response Safety Evaluation ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, SingProbe with Ling-3.0-flash achieves the best average F1 of 0.8728, outperforming the strongest standalone baseline, Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B-strict, by 1.24 points. Under the matched intrinsic-guard setting with Ling-3.0-flash, it also exceeds Vanilla (0.8535), CC++ (0.8652), and Kelp (0.8630) by 1.93, 0.76, and 0.98 points, respectively. SingProbe with Ling-3.0-tiny remains competitive at 0.8508, and scaling from Ling-3.0-tiny to Ling-3.0-flash yields consistent gains across nearly all benchmarks. In particular, SingProbe with Ling-3.0-flash achieves the best F1 on WildGuard (0.8000) and XGuard Test (0.8588), while CC++ obtains the highest score on ExpGuardTest (0.9253).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">

</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Streaming Safety Detection.</span> Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Response Safety Evaluation ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> evaluates detection throughout generation on SingStreamBench, SingStreamBench-Full, and FineHarm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025c</a>)</cite>. Response-level AUC (R-AUC) is computed using the maximum response-safety score over all token positions and takes the response-level label as the ground-truth label, whereas token-level AUC (T-AUC) directly evaluates the score at each token position against the corresponding fine-grained annotation. The tokens in the annotated safe prefix are labeled as <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>. Since streaming detection primarily concerns token-level risk localization, we use average T-AUC as the principal metric. All intrinsic-guard configurations outperform the Qwen3Guard-Stream baselines in both average R-AUC and T-AUC. The best streaming configuration is Ling-3.0-flash-singprobe, which obtains the highest average T-AUC of 0.9481 together with an R-AUC of 0.9887. Ling-3.0-tiny-singprobe obtains a comparable 0.9888/0.9479 R-AUC/T-AUC. Relative to the strongest Qwen3Guard-Stream baseline, Ling-3.0-flash-singprobe improves average T-AUC by 4.93 percentage points, while Kelp achieves the highest average R-AUC of 0.9912, a 2.72-point improvement. In the matched intrinsic-guard comparison, Vanilla obtains 0.9739/0.9228 R-AUC/T-AUC, CC++ obtains 0.9875/0.9478, and Kelp obtains 0.9912/0.9193. Thus, the SingProbe objectives substantially improve both response- and token-level detection over uniform BCE. Compared with CC++, Ling-3.0-flash-singprobe further improves average R-AUC and T-AUC to 0.9887 and 0.9481, respectively; Kelp instead prioritizes response-level discrimination at the cost of substantially lower token-level localization. The improvements over external streaming baselines are especially pronounced on SingStreamBench and SingStreamBench-Full, while performance remains comparable on FineHarm.</p>
</div>

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">False-positive Evaluation.</span> We additionally evaluate false alarms under free generation using five nominally benign datasets. These datasets are MATH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, databricks-dolly-15k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Conover et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, MBPP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Austin et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, and OpenBookQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mihaylov et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. Each model receives a query and generates its own response, during which we collect both query-intent and response-safety scores; the final predictions use the same aggregation rules described above. Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Response Safety Evaluation ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> reports query/response FPR in each cell and macro averages across the five datasets. SingProbe maintains a low macro-average response FPR, with 0.04% on Ling-3.0-tiny and 0.01% on Ling-3.0-flash, on par with the strongest Qwen3Guard-Stream baselines. The matched intrinsic baselines also retain a 0.01% macro-average response FPR; their query FPRs are 0.08% for Vanilla and CC++, and 0.28% for Kelp, compared with 0.08% for SingProbe with Ling-3.0-flash. We note that these datasets are not exhaustively safety-audited and may contain a small number of genuinely unsafe queries or responses. The reported values should therefore be interpreted as apparent FPRs and may slightly overestimate the true false-positive rates.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">

<td id="S4.T6.6.1.13.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">0.5996</td>
<td id="S4.T6.6.1.13.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">0.7282</td>
<td id="S4.T6.6.1.13.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T6.6.1.13.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.7314</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.6.1.13.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">0.9674</td>
<td id="S4.T6.6.1.13.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EBFFEB;"><span id="S4.T6.6.1.13.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EBFFEB;">0.8012</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate response-level hallucination detection on six offline benchmarks (FactCHD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, FaithDial <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dziri et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, FAVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mishra et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, RAGTruth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Shroom <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mickus et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and WikiBio <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Manakul et al., 2023</a>)</cite>). Given a query-response pair, SingProbe produces a hallucination score at every response token under teacher forcing. We use the maximum score over all response positions as the response-level risk score and compute ROC AUC across samples. Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.4 Response Hallucination Evaluation ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> reports the per-benchmark results and their macro average.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">SingProbe achieves strong and consistent performance across both base models. On Ling-3.0-tiny, SingProbe obtains the best average AUC of 0.7765, outperforming the strongest baseline, DRIFT, by 3.57 points, and achieves the best per-benchmark AUC on FactCHD (0.7819), FaithDial (0.9529), and WikiBio (0.9515). Scaling to Ling-3.0-flash further improves SingProbe to 0.8012, outperforming the best baseline DRIFT (0.8000). These results indicate that the hidden states of the base model provide effective signals for hallucination detection and that their quality improves with model scale, enabling a lightweight intrinsic head to be competitive with or surpass specialized hallucination detectors.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Overhead Evaluation</h3>

TTFT denotes time to first token, and ITL denotes inter-token latency. <span id="S4.T7.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Decode Probe</span> runs SingProbe only during decoding, while <span id="S4.T7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Prefill-enabled Probe</span> additionally runs SingProbe during the prefill stage. Positive values indicate additional overhead relative to the base model without SingProbe.</figcaption>

</table>

</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the inference overhead introduced by SingProbe (with the unified architecture on Ling-3.0-flash) under a controlled serving-load protocol. Each request uses an input length of 8,192 tokens and an output length of 1,024 tokens, and we vary the concurrency from 1 to 32. At each concurrency level, we submit a fixed number of prompts per round (24 for concurrency 1, 2, and 4; 48 for concurrency 8; and 96 for concurrency 16 and 32) and repeat the measurement over 8 independent rounds. Within each round, we compute the median TTFT and ITL, pair each SingProbe-enabled configuration with the base-model-only baseline of the same round, and report the mean and standard deviation of the paired relative differences across rounds. We consider two deployment modes of SingProbe: <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Decode Probe</span>, which runs the probe only during autoregressive decoding, and <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Prefill-enabled Probe</span>, which additionally invokes the probe during the prefill stage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 4.5 Overhead Evaluation ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, the additional latency introduced by SingProbe remains small across all concurrency levels. For the <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Decode Probe</span> configuration, the ITL overhead is consistently below <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5\%</annotation></semantics></math>, ranging from <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.18\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>0.18</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.18\%</annotation></semantics></math> at concurrency 1 to <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.45\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>0.45</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.45\%</annotation></semantics></math> at concurrency 32. The TTFT differences are within measurement noise: they are typically within <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 1.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 1.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> and even show slightly negative point estimates at concurrency 2 and 4, with standard deviations that comfortably span zero. This is expected because the decode-only probe does not participate in the prefill phase and therefore should not change TTFT in a systematic way. Enabling the probe during prefill (<span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Prefill-enabled Probe</span>) adds a small but consistently positive TTFT overhead, ranging from <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.86\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>0.86</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.86\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+2.25\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2.25</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+2.25\%</annotation></semantics></math>, while the ITL overhead remains essentially unchanged and below <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S4.SS5.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.18\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>0.18</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.18\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.47\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>0.47</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.47\%</annotation></semantics></math>). Overall, the relative overhead does not grow with serving concurrency, and even in the more expensive prefill-enabled setting the additional cost stays around <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.SS5.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\%</annotation></semantics></math> on TTFT and well under <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> on ITL. These results demonstrate that continuously extracting guardrail signals from the base model’s hidden states introduces little additional cost to either first-token latency or token-by-token decoding, and that this overhead remains stable under increasing serving load. This efficiency supports the practical deployment of SingProbe as an intrinsic streaming guardrail without requiring a separate guardrail inference service.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>Ablaton Study of the Number of Tapped Layers</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We ablate the number of hidden layers tapped from the frozen base model, varying <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L\in\{1,2,3,5,8\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L\in\{1,2,3,5,8\}</annotation></semantics></math> while keeping the Guard architecture and training recipe fixed. As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.6 Ablaton Study of the Number of Tapped Layers ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, safety detection is generally robust to the number of tapped layers. Query AUC remains within a narrow range of <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9560" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9560</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9560</annotation></semantics></math>-<math id="S4.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9579" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9579</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9579</annotation></semantics></math>, while Response AUC varies from <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9648" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9648</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9648</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9684" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9684</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9684</annotation></semantics></math>. Notably, using only the final layer already yields strong performance, achieving a Response AUC of <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9648" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9648</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9648</annotation></semantics></math> and a streaming response AUC of <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9767" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9767</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9767</annotation></semantics></math>. Incorporating intermediate-layer representations nevertheless provides modest improvements: compared with <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L{=}1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L{=}1</annotation></semantics></math>, the <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L{=}3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L{=}3</annotation></semantics></math> configuration improves Response AUC from <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9648" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9648</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9648</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9677" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9677</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9677</annotation></semantics></math> and streaming response AUC from <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9767" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9767</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9767</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9823" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9823</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9823</annotation></semantics></math>. Hallucination detection benefits more clearly from multi-layer features, with AUC increasing from <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.7750" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.7750</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.7750</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L{=}1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L{=}1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.7963" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.7963</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.7963</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L{=}3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L{=}3</annotation></semantics></math> and reaching <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.7988" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.7988</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.7988</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L{=}8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L{=}8</annotation></semantics></math>. This suggests that hallucination detection may require information that is less completely captured by the final-layer representation. Across all configurations, the benign false-positive rate remains at or below <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.02\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.02</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.02\%</annotation></semantics></math>, indicating that tapping additional layers does not noticeably increase over-triggering on benign inputs. However, tapping more layers increases the input dimensionality of the Guard, leading to a larger parameter count, higher memory consumption, and additional inference latency. Since the performance gains become marginal beyond <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L{=}3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L{=}3</annotation></semantics></math> while these deployment costs continue to grow, we use three tapped layers by default to achieve a favorable effectiveness–efficiency trade-off.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2608.30703v2/layer_ablation_bar.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/157;" width="471" height="157"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>The ablation study of the number of tapped base-model layers.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.7 </span>Generation-time Applications of SingProbe</h3>

<section id="S4.SS7.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.7.1 </span>Application 1: SingProbe for Online Content Detection</h4>

<div id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The preceding evaluations are conducted offline: each detector receives a fixed query–response pair under teacher forcing, allowing its predictions to be compared against pre-existing labels. In practical deployment, however, the base model generates responses autoregressively, and the guardrail must assess content produced by the model itself as generation unfolds. We therefore conduct an online evaluation in which Ling-3.0 freely generates responses while SingProbe produces detection signals alongside decoding. We study this setting for both response safety and hallucination detection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Online Safety Detection.</span> We compare SingProbe with GPT-OSS-120B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agarwal et al., 2025</a>)</cite> (as an LLM judger), Qwen3Guard-Stream-8B, and YuFeng-XGuard-Reason-8B on HarmBench, WildGuard, and XSTest. Because the safety labels of freely generated responses are not available a priori, we adopt a leave-one-out evaluation protocol. For each evaluated detector, the majority vote of the other three detectors is used as its pseudo-ground-truth label, ensuring that the evaluated detector does not contribute to its own reference label. We then report Accuracy and F1 against this leave-one-out consensus.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 4.7.1 Application 1: SingProbe for Online Content Detection ‣ 4.7 Generation-time Applications of SingProbe ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, SingProbe performance improves substantially with a stronger base model. With Ling-3.0-tiny, SingProbe obtains an average Accuracy of 0.8089 and an average F1 of 0.4726, which trails the stronger standalone baselines under this leave-one-out protocol. With Ling-3.0-flash, however, SingProbe delivers the strongest overall performance, reaching an average Accuracy of 0.9641 and an average F1 of 0.6452. It outperforms the strongest baseline average F1 (YuFeng-XGuard-Reason-8B at 0.5964) by 4.88 points and obtains the best F1 on both WildGuard (0.6364) and XSTest (0.5405). These results demonstrate that SingProbe remains effective when its predictions are produced during free autoregressive generation, rather than from fixed responses under teacher forcing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Note that the comparatively modest F1 scores are largely attributable to the severe class imbalance in this online setting: most freely generated responses are Safe, leaving relatively few Unsafe examples. Under such a low positive-class prevalence, even a small number of false positives or disagreements among the detectors can substantially reduce precision and, consequently, the F1 score. The online F1 values should therefore be interpreted together with Accuracy and primarily used for relative comparison among methods evaluated under the same protocol, rather than directly compared with results on more balanced offline benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T8" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 8: </span>Online response safety detection under free autoregressive generation. For each evaluated detector, pseudo-ground-truth labels are obtained by majority vote of the other three detectors under a leave-one-out protocol. The SingProbe detector is evaluated with its bias-calibrated checkpoint at the canonical 0.5 decision threshold. Values report Accuracy (Acc) and F1. The best result within each backbone is highlighted in bold.</figcaption>

<td id="S4.T9.2.1.10.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">0.5802</td>

<td id="S4.T9.2.1.10.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EBFFEB;padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S4.T9.2.1.10.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EBFFEB;">0.6193</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T9.2.1.11" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S4.T9.2.1.11.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">0.6799</td>

</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Online Hallucination Detection.</span> In the online hallucination evaluation, the model first performs autoregressive rollout on each test set to generate responses. An LLM, specifically Qwen3.5-397B-A17B in our experiments, then judges whether each response is correct based on the question, the model response, and the ground-truth answer, producing a binary label of whether hallucination occurs. Using these labels, we compute the hallucination-detection AUC for five methods: DRIFT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhatnagar et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, HaMI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, SAPLMA-raw, SAPLMA-response <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Azaria and Mitchell, 2023</a>)</cite>, and SingProbe, across seven datasets: AA-Omniscience <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jackson et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, BBH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, MATH-500 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, NQ-Open <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, SQuAD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rajpurkar et al., 2016</a>)</cite>, and TruthfulQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Results are reported on two backbones, Ling-3.0-tiny and Ling-3.0-flash.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The results show that SingProbe achieves a clear and consistent advantage on both backbones, attaining the best average AUC in every case. On Ling-3.0-tiny, it reaches 0.6786, leading the second-best method DRIFT (0.6316) by an absolute margin of 0.047. On Ling-3.0-flash, it reaches 0.7271, leading DRIFT (0.6546) by 0.073. As backbone capability increases, SingProbe’s performance improves from 0.6786 to 0.7271, and its lead over the second-best method widens further, indicating that SingProbe can make fuller use of the internal signals from stronger backbone models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">SingProbe’s advantage is also evident on individual datasets. On Ling-3.0-flash, SingProbe ranks first on five of the seven datasets: AA-Omniscience, GSM8K, MATH-500, NQ-Open, and SQuAD. Among them, the AUC on four datasets, AA-Omniscience, GSM8K, MATH-500, and SQuAD, exceeds 0.73, with SQuAD reaching 0.8597. On Ling-3.0-tiny, SingProbe also leads comprehensively on knowledge- or reasoning-intensive tasks such as GSM8K, MATH-500, and NQ-Open, achieving 0.7328, 0.7292, and 0.8136, respectively. In contrast, the baselines achieve local best results only on a few individual datasets and do not show a consistent advantage across backbones. Although SAPLMA-response performs relatively well on some BBH and TruthfulQA settings, its average AUC is 0.067 lower than SingProbe on tiny and 0.089 lower on flash; the gaps for HaMI and SAPLMA-raw are even larger.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS7.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.7.2 </span>Application 2: SingProbe for Constrained Safe Decoding</h4>

<div id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond detecting unsafe content that has already appeared, an intrinsic streaming guardrail may also reveal how the safety of a response is likely to evolve. We study this possibility through two sequential research questions. First, <em id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">can SingProbe predict the safety tendency of future generations from the current prefix?</em> Second, if the score is predictive of future risk, <em id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">can it be used to guide safe decoding by terminating risky branches before they continue?</em> Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.7.2 Application 2: SingProbe for Constrained Safe Decoding ‣ 4.7 Generation-time Applications of SingProbe ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> summarizes the corresponding rollout prediction and branch-pruning experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experimental Settings.</span> We use Ling-3.0-flash as the frozen generation model and its SingProbe head as the safety probe. The response-unsafety score is streamed directly from the hidden states produced during decoding through the same SGLang serving pipeline, without an additional forward pass. For every evaluated prefix, we sample eight continuations. An independent YuFeng-XGuard-Reason-8B judge assigns a binary Safe or Unsafe label to each completed rollout. It is worth noting that the safety of the generated responses is assessed by an external judge and therefore may not constitute ground-truth labels. Nevertheless, the observed increase or decrease in the unsafe response rate still provides meaningful evidence of SingProbe’s contribution to safety.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Can SingProbe predict future generation risk?</span> We operationalize this question by testing whether the score at the current <em id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">safe</em> prefix correlates with the fraction of future continuations that eventually become unsafe. Specifically, we collect 500 query–prefix pairs, including 350 unsafe-origin and 150 safe-origin examples. Each input consists of a query followed by an annotated safe response prefix, allowing us to test whether SingProbe can anticipate a future transition to unsafe content while the observed response remains safe. We record SingProbe’s response-unsafety score at the final token of this safe prefix, before any further continuation is sampled, and then generate eight independent rollouts. Their judged labels define the empirical future unsafe rate of the query–prefix pair, <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}_{\mathrm{unsafe}}=n_{\mathrm{unsafe}}/8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>unsafe</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>unsafe</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}_{\mathrm{unsafe}}=n_{\mathrm{unsafe}}/8</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F4.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2608.30703v2/fig/rollout_bar.png" id="S4.F4.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/313;" width="476" height="313" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span>Predicting future generation risk from annotated safe prefixes.
Starting from each query and its annotated safe response prefix, we group subsequent rollouts by the SingProbe score at the final safe-prefix token and report the empirical unsafe rates of their rollouts. Higher safe-prefix scores consistently correspond to greater unsafe risk in future continuations.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F4.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2608.30703v2/fig/chunk_prune.png" id="S4.F4.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/313;" width="476" height="313" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span>SingProbe-guided branch pruning from annotated safe prefixes.
Starting from each query and its annotated safe response prefix, we sample intermediate chunks to form candidate decoding branches. Branches with the highest chunk-end SingProbe scores are pruned before further continuation. The resulting policy substantially reduces the unsafe rate compared with greedy sampling and random pruning and closely approaches the optimal.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Anticipatory safety prediction and constrained safe decoding with SingProbe.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F4.sf1" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 4.7.2 Application 2: SingProbe for Constrained Safe Decoding ‣ 4.7 Generation-time Applications of SingProbe ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(a)</span></a> shows a clear monotonic relationship between the safe-prefix score and subsequent rollout safety. The empirical unsafe rate rises from approximately <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.02" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.02</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.02</annotation></semantics></math> in the lowest-score interval to <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.43" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.43</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.43</annotation></semantics></math> in the highest, which is roughly <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.6\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.6\times</annotation></semantics></math> the overall base rate of <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1203" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.1203</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1203</annotation></semantics></math> and over <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="21\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>21</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">21\times</annotation></semantics></math> the rate in the lowest-score group. The increase becomes particularly pronounced in the higher-score intervals, rising from <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.08" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.08</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.08</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.14" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.14</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.14</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.16</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.20</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.20</annotation></semantics></math>, and finally <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.43" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.43</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.43</annotation></semantics></math>. Because every observed prefix is annotated as safe and the score is recorded before continuation, this trend cannot be explained by SingProbe merely reacting to harmful content that has already appeared. Instead, it indicates that the hidden state at a safe prefix contains information about the conditional safety tendency of its possible continuations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Can SingProbe guide safe decoding?</span> Motivated by this predictive relationship, we next test whether the score can identify risky decoding branches early enough to prune them. As in the first experiment, each root consists of a query followed by an annotated safe response prefix. We select 16 conflict query–prefix roots for which three to five of the initial eight rollouts are unsafe, ensuring that every root admits both safe and unsafe continuations. Starting from each query and safe prefix, we sample 24 distinct 64-token chunks, yielding 384 intermediate branch prefixes. At the end of each chunk, we record SingProbe’s response-unsafety score before sampling any further tokens and then generate eight continuations, producing 3,072 judged rollouts.
We simulate constrained decoding by removing the fraction <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> of branches with the highest SingProbe unsafety scores and measuring the unsafe rate among continuations from the retained branches. As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F4.sf2" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 4.7.2 Application 2: SingProbe for Constrained Safe Decoding ‣ 4.7 Generation-time Applications of SingProbe ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(b)</span></a>, this SingProbe-guided policy is compared with random pruning averaged over 200 permutations and an empirical-risk oracle that removes branches with the highest observed unsafe rates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Guard-guided pruning consistently reduces the unsafe rate of the retained rollout pool, whereas random pruning leaves it nearly unchanged at approximately <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.76" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.76</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.76</annotation></semantics></math>. When pruning <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the branches, SingProbe lowers the retained-pool unsafe rate to <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.53" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.53</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.53</annotation></semantics></math>, a relative reduction of approximately <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\%</annotation></semantics></math> compared with random pruning, and essentially matches the oracle rate of <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.53" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.53</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.53</annotation></semantics></math>. The unsafe rate continues to decrease as more high-scoring branches are removed, reaching approximately <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.22" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.22</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.22</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> of branches are pruned. The SingProbe and oracle curves nearly overlap up to a pruning fraction of about <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math> and diverge only at aggressive pruning ratios, where the oracle drops toward <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> while SingProbe plateaus around <math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.22" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.22</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.22</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.SS7.SSS2.p6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.23" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.23</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.23</annotation></semantics></math>. This suggests that SingProbe is highly accurate at identifying the highest-risk branches but is less precise in ranking the remaining lower-risk branches. Overall, these results demonstrate that SingProbe’s anticipatory signal is not only correlated with future safety outcomes but can also serve as a practical control signal for constrained safe decoding.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>SingProbe-Med: On-Demand Medical-Risk Intervention</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Motivation and Framework Overview</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The preceding sections introduce SingProbe as a lightweight guardrail for a frozen LLM during autoregressive generation. We now study how such token-level internal-state signals can be used not only for detection, but also to control <em id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">when</em> a generation-time intervention should modify subsequent decoding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Medical generation provides a representative setting in which selective intervention is particularly important. A harmful recommendation may emerge only after a clinically sound prefix, making query-level screening insufficient and post-hoc review too late to prevent the error from being generated <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singhal et al., 2023</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Draelos et al., 2026</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mishra et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>. At the same time, applying a corrective decoding mechanism throughout the entire response is undesirable: always-on steering can perturb otherwise correct medical content and incurs persistent decoding cost. An effective intervention system should therefore answer two complementary questions: <em id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">when should intervention be activated, and how should generation be modified once intervention is needed?</em></p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2608.30703v2/fig-0822.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:438/293;" width="438" height="293" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="S5.F5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SingProbe-Med intervention overview.</span> (a) Once admitted, target-supported sGDS contrasts target and medical risk-pattern logits while keeping both branches synchronized through a shared sampled token. (b) Future- or Boundary-based activation opens a bounded intervention window, after which generation returns to native decoding.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">SingProbe-Med separates these two responsibilities. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.1 Motivation and Framework Overview ‣ 5 SingProbe-Med: On-Demand Medical-Risk Intervention ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, SingProbe-Med is responsible for deciding when to intervene by continuously monitoring the evolving generation trajectory through lightweight internal-state signals. Once the admission condition is satisfied, a target-supported intervention mechanism named support-constrained Guided Decoding Steering (sGDS) determines how to intervene by contrastively re-ranking the target model’s candidate tokens over a localized risky suffix. The intervention is bounded in duration, after which generation returns to the target model’s native decoding. This design separates inexpensive continuous monitoring from the more expensive corrective decoding mechanism, avoiding persistent dual-branch inference on generations for which no intervention is needed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We instantiate this framework on AntAngelMed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">AntAngelMed Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, a 100B-parameter MoE medical LLM. We next describe the two components separately: the SingProbe-Med admission mechanism for determining <em id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">when to intervene</em>, followed by target-supported sGDS for determining <em id="S5.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how to intervene</em>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>SingProbe-Med: When to Intervene</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At decoding step <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, SingProbe-Med derives four complementary signals from the current prefix <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{\leq t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{\leq t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Rather than serving as independent prediction tasks, these signals correspond to different decisions required by the intervention controller. The semantics of the four signals are summarized in Table <a href="#S5.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ 5.2 SingProbe-Med: When to Intervene ‣ 5 SingProbe-Med: On-Demand Medical-Risk Intervention ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>.</p>
<ul id="S5.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Intervention Eligibility <math id="S5.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{t}</annotation></semantics></math></span> determines whether the current prefix contains a clinically consequential proposition for which medical-risk intervention is applicable.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Global Risk <math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{t}</annotation></semantics></math></span> estimates whether the evolving response trajectory is moving toward a harmful medical conclusion. The remaining two signals provide more localized timing information.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Future Risk <math id="S5.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}</annotation></semantics></math></span> indicates whether a confirmable medical error is likely to emerge within the next 1–32 tokens, enabling intervention before the error is committed.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Error Boundary <math id="S5.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{t}</annotation></semantics></math></span> identifies the first prefix at which a medical error becomes confirmable, allowing immediate containment when sufficiently early predictive evidence is unavailable.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T10" class="ltx_table">
