<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These signals are combined through a fixed evidential hierarchy to form an admission policy. Intervention of the next uncommitted token is activated according to</p>
<table id="S5.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="a_{t+1}=\mathbb{I}\left[E_{t}\geq\gamma_{E}\;\wedge\;\left(G_{t}\geq\gamma_{G}\;\vee\;\left(G_{t}\geq\gamma_{C}\wedge\left(F_{t}\geq\gamma_{F}\vee B_{t}\geq\gamma_{B}\right)\right)\right)\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝕀</mi><mrow><mo>[</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>E</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.502em">∧</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>G</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.502em">∨</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>∧</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mo>∨</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t+1}=\mathbb{I}\left[E_{t}\geq\gamma_{E}\;\wedge\;\left(G_{t}\geq\gamma_{G}\;\vee\;\left(G_{t}\geq\gamma_{C}\wedge\left(F_{t}\geq\gamma_{F}\vee B_{t}\geq\gamma_{B}\right)\right)\right)\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This rule follows an <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E\rightarrow G\rightarrow(F/B)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E\rightarrow G\rightarrow(F/B)</annotation></semantics></math> hierarchy motivated by the asymmetric cost of false intervention. <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> first restricts intervention to prefixes for which risk-directed steering is applicable. <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> then provides trajectory-level evidence of emerging medical harm. When the global-risk signal is sufficiently strong, intervention can be admitted directly to avoid unnecessary delay. Under intermediate global evidence, the shorter-horizon <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> signals refine the intervention timing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Importantly, <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are complementary entry signals rather than sequential stages. <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> supports <em id="S5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">anticipatory intervention</em> before a medical error becomes explicit, whereas <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> provides <em id="S5.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">boundary-level containment</em> at the earliest prefix where the error can be confirmed. All four signals are computed in parallel; the hierarchy therefore specifies evidential precedence rather than a sequential execution pipeline. The operating thresholds and release conditions are fixed on the development split before final evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Target-Supported sGDS: How to Intervene</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Once SingProbe-Med determines that intervention is warranted, we steer the subsequent generation by explicitly modeling and suppressing medical-risk preferences in the decoding distribution. Specifically, we construct a risk-pattern branch by adapting the target model with a medical-risk LoRA adapter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, and use the difference between the target and risk-pattern logits to guide contrastive intervention. In the following sections, we first define the medical-risk patterns covered by the intervention. We then describe how the corresponding risk-pattern branch is constructed and how its logits are incorporated into target-supported sGDS.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Medical-risk Intervention Scope.</span>
We define the intervention scope using five operational medical-risk categories: dosage and administration errors, special-population contraindications, wrong indications, dermatology-specific wrong indications, and dermatology-specific special-population contraindications. These categories are used to organize the risk-pattern adaptation data and jointly construct the training set for the medical intervention branch. The sampler maintains approximately balanced coverage across the five categories. Table <a href="#S5.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ 5.3 Target-Supported sGDS: How to Intervene ‣ 5 SingProbe-Med: On-Demand Medical-Risk Intervention ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> summarizes the corresponding intervention targets. The resulting risk-pattern dataset is used to adapt the medical intervention branch described next.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T11" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 11: </span>Medical-risk categories covered by the intervention branch.</figcaption>

<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Medical Risk-pattern Branch.</span>
We construct the medical risk-pattern branch by adapting the deployed AntAngelMed model with a LoRA module on the risk-pattern dataset described above. The adaptation follows a standard supervised fine-tuning style objective: given a medical prompt <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and a risk-pattern response <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T})</annotation></semantics></math>, we optimize only the LoRA parameters <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\mathrm{risk}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>risk</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\mathrm{risk}}</annotation></semantics></math> while keeping the base-model parameters <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> frozen. Specifically, the branch is trained with the autoregressive language-modeling loss</p>
<table id="S5.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E9.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{risk}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\theta+\Delta_{\mathrm{risk}}}\left(y_{t}\mid x,y_{&lt;t}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>risk</mi></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>risk</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{risk}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\theta+\Delta_{\mathrm{risk}}}\left(y_{t}\mid x,y_{&lt;t}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where the training responses are drawn from the five medical-risk categories defined above. Optimizing this objective increases the adapted branch’s likelihood on continuations that exhibit the corresponding medical-risk patterns, thereby encoding these patterns into the learned LoRA parameters.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">After adaptation, the original model and the risk-pattern-adapted model form the two branches used during intervention. Let <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the original AntAngelMed model and <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\mathrm{risk}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>risk</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\mathrm{risk}}</annotation></semantics></math> the learned medical-risk LoRA parameters. Given the realized decoding context <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}=(x,y_{\leq t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}=(x,y_{\leq t})</annotation></semantics></math>, they produce next-token logits as</p>
<table id="S5.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t+1}=f_{\theta}(c_{t}),\qquad\ell^{\mathrm{risk}}_{t+1}=f_{\theta+\Delta_{\mathrm{risk}}}(c_{t})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>tar</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>risk</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>risk</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t+1}=f_{\theta}(c_{t}),\qquad\ell^{\mathrm{risk}}_{t+1}=f_{\theta+\Delta_{\mathrm{risk}}}(c_{t}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Because the adapted branch is explicitly trained on risk-pattern continuations, it assigns relatively greater support to tokens and continuations that are compatible with the covered medical-risk patterns. We therefore use it as an <em id="S5.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">anti-expert</em>: <math id="S5.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell^{\mathrm{risk}}_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>risk</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{\mathrm{risk}}_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math> provides a token-level risk preference that can be contrasted with the target-model logits during intervention, rather than being interpreted as an explicit medical-error probability or an independently generated correction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">On-demand Target-supported sGDS.</span>
With the medical risk-pattern branch defined above, we use its next-token logits as an anti-expert signal to modify the target model only when intervention is activated. At each activated decoding step, the target and risk-pattern branches evaluate the same realized context <math id="S5.SS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}=(x,y_{\leq t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}=(x,y_{\leq t})</annotation></semantics></math>, producing <math id="S5.SS3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>tar</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS3.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell^{\mathrm{risk}}_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>risk</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{\mathrm{risk}}_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math> for the same uncommitted token. We then contrast these two distributions while restricting the intervention to candidates already supported by the target model. Specifically, the target branch first defines the admissible candidate set</p>
<table id="S5.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{t+1}=\operatorname{TopK}\left(\ell^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t+1},k\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>TopK</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>tar</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{t+1}=\operatorname{TopK}\left(\ell^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t+1},k\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS3.p6.2" class="ltx_p">Within this support, sGDS computes</p>
<table id="S5.E12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell^{\mathrm{sGDS}}_{t+1}(v)=\begin{cases}(1+\alpha)\ell^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t+1}(v)-\alpha\ell^{\mathrm{risk}}_{t+1}(v),&amp;v\in C_{t+1},\\
-\infty,&amp;v\notin C_{t+1}.\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>sGDS</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>tar</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>risk</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∉</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{\mathrm{sGDS}}_{t+1}(v)=\begin{cases}(1+\alpha)\ell^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t+1}(v)-\alpha\ell^{\mathrm{risk}}_{t+1}(v),&amp;v\in C_{t+1},\\
-\infty,&amp;v\notin C_{t+1}.\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS3.p6.3" class="ltx_p">The resulting <math id="S5.SS3.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell^{\mathrm{sGDS}}_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>sGDS</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{\mathrm{sGDS}}_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math> serves as the final next-token logits, from which the sampling distribution is obtained and the next token is selected. Equivalently, sGDS adds the contrastive direction <math id="S5.SS3.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha(\ell^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t+1}-\ell^{\mathrm{risk}}_{t+1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>tar</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>risk</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha(\ell^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t+1}-\ell^{\mathrm{risk}}_{t+1})</annotation></semantics></math> to the native target logits within <math id="S5.SS3.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math>. Since the risk-pattern branch is adapted to favor continuations exhibiting the covered medical-risk patterns, candidates that receive relatively stronger support from this branch are suppressed, while candidates favored more strongly by the target branch are promoted relative to their competitors. The top-<math id="S5.SS3.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> restriction keeps the target model as the source of admissible next tokens, so the risk branch only re-ranks plausible target-supported candidates rather than introducing its own off-support continuations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The two branches operate as paired conditional scorers rather than independently decoded models. They begin from the same prompt and realized response prefix while maintaining separate model states and KV caches. At each activated step, a single token <math id="S5.SS3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math> is sampled from the fused sGDS distribution and appended to both branches. This shared-token update keeps their prefixes synchronized, ensuring that subsequent target and risk-pattern logits continue to describe the same generation history. If the branches were decoded independently, their prefixes would diverge and the resulting logit difference would no longer isolate the learned risk preference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">When <math id="S5.SS3.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t+1}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t+1}=0</annotation></semantics></math>, generation proceeds directly from the unmodified target-model logits and the risk-pattern branch does not participate in logit fusion. Once intervention is activated, it opens an intervention episode</p>
<table id="S5.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e=(\tau,W,k,\alpha)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>W</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e=(\tau,W,k,\alpha),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS3.p8.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS3.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the activation position, <math id="S5.SS3.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> bounds the intervention duration, <math id="S5.SS3.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> determines the target-supported candidate set, and <math id="S5.SS3.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> controls the strength of the contrastive correction. We evaluate both a full intervention and a bounded variant. The full intervention uses <math id="S5.SS3.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=50</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS3.p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math> until release, whereas the bounded variant uses <math id="S5.SS3.p8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=100</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS3.p8.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=3</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.SS3.p8.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=64</annotation></semantics></math>. After the episode is released, decoding returns to target-only logits on the already modified prefix.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Thus, the intervention is on demand at two levels. SingProbe-Med determines <em id="S5.SS3.p9.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">when</em> the more expensive dual-branch decoding should be activated, while target-supported sGDS determines <em id="S5.SS3.p9.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> the next-token distribution should be modified once activated. By confining both the activation interval and the admissible vocabulary, the resulting intervention suppresses learned medical-risk preferences only over the risk-relevant portion of generation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate SingProbe-Med along four complementary quantitative axes: admission selectivity and timing, medical error correction, general capability preservation, and inference efficiency. We further provide a qualitative case study to illustrate how the resulting intervention modifies representative medical-risk continuations. All admission thresholds and episode-release conditions are selected on the development split and frozen before evaluation on the held-out medical set. No threshold is reselected on the test set or separately for an individual capability benchmark.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.4.1 </span>Admission Selectivity and Timing</h4>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first evaluate whether the admission mechanism can identify trajectories that warrant intervention and trigger sufficiently early. “Harm” denotes a trajectory containing a target medical risk, whereas “White” denotes a trajectory for which intervention should not be triggered. Let <math id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> indicate whether trajectory <math id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> opens at least one intervention episode. At a fixed operating point, we report</p>
<table id="S5.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E14.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\left\{\begin{aligned} \mathrm{White\ FPR}&amp;=\Pr(A_{i}=1\mid i\in\mathrm{White}),\\
\mathrm{Harm\ recall}&amp;=\Pr(A_{i}=1\mid i\in\mathrm{Harm}),\\
\mathrm{Precision}&amp;=\Pr(i\in\mathrm{Harm}\mid A_{i}=1).\end{aligned}\right." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>White</mi><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>FPR</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>White</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>Harm</mi><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>recall</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Harm</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mi>Precision</mi></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Harm</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\{\begin{aligned} \mathrm{White\ FPR}&amp;=\Pr(A_{i}=1\mid i\in\mathrm{White}),\\
\mathrm{Harm\ recall}&amp;=\Pr(A_{i}=1\mid i\in\mathrm{Harm}),\\
\mathrm{Precision}&amp;=\Pr(i\in\mathrm{Harm}\mid A_{i}=1).\end{aligned}\right.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We additionally report ROC–AUC, Average Precision (AP), and PR–AUC from the complete trajectory-level ranking on the held-out set. For the White-FPR operating points <math id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in\{10\%,5\%,1\%\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q\in\{10\%,5\%,1\%\}</annotation></semantics></math>, thresholds are selected on the development set and frozen before evaluating Harm recall and precision on the held-out set.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the combined detector, Intervention Eligibility acts as a binary gate on the Global Risk score. Specifically, we define the gated risk score as</p>
<table id="S5.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{E+G}=\mathbb{I}(E&gt;\gamma_{E})\,\sigma(G)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>E</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{E+G}=\mathbb{I}(E&gt;\gamma_{E})\,\sigma(G),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>E</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{E}</annotation></semantics></math> is the Intervention Eligibility threshold and <math id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the sigmoid function. Thus, Global Risk contributes to the ranking only when the corresponding prefix is considered eligible for medical-risk intervention.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ 5.4.1 Admission Selectivity and Timing ‣ 5.4 Evaluation ‣ 5 SingProbe-Med: On-Demand Medical-Risk Intervention ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> compares Global Risk alone with this eligibility-gated Global Risk score. Applying the Intervention Eligibility gate improves ROC–AUC, AP, and PR–AUC by 0.025, 0.012, and 0.011, respectively, indicating that suppressing risk scores on intervention-ineligible prefixes improves trajectory selection. Tightening the allowed White FPR from 10% to 1% increases precision from 92.34% to 96.77%, while Harm recall decreases from 51.70% to 11.98%, exposing a direct trade-off between intervention coverage and false-trigger control.</p>
</div>

</div></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<div id="S5.T12.3" class="ltx_block ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:124.2pt;">
<p id="S5.T12.3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.T12.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b) Constrained operating points (%)</span></p>
<table id="S5.T12.3.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S5.T12.3.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T12.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:0.4pt;padding-bottom:0.4pt;">
<span id="S5.T12.3.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S5.T12.3.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">White FPR</span>
</span></th>
<th id="S5.T12.3.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:0.4pt;padding-bottom:0.4pt;">Harm recall</th>
<th id="S5.T12.3.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:0.4pt;padding-bottom:0.4pt;">Precision</th></tr>
</thead>

</table>
</div></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We further evaluate activation timing on Harm trajectories with a confirmable medical error boundary. Let <math id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{\mathrm{confirm}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>T</mi><mi>confirm</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{\mathrm{confirm}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the first prefix at which the medical error becomes confirmable. Among Harm trajectories, 54.99% of first activations occur at or before <math id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{\mathrm{confirm}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>T</mi><mi>confirm</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{\mathrm{confirm}}</annotation></semantics></math>, meaning that the policy opens a correction window no later than the confirmable error boundary for more than half of the risky trajectories. Evaluating all four SingProbe-Med signals over 3,044,056 token states takes 0.019749 ms/token, corresponding to approximately 50,635 token states per second.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T13" class="ltx_table">

<section id="S5.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.4.2 </span>Medical Error Correction</h4>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next evaluate whether an admitted intervention corrects the final medical outcome. Each test case is matched by prompt between target-only decoding and an intervention configuration. Let <math id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{i}^{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{i}^{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{i}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{i}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the three-way adjudicated outcomes of the baseline and intervened responses in <math id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathrm{ERROR},\mathrm{SAFE},\mathrm{UNCERTAIN}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>ERROR</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>SAFE</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>UNCERTAIN</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathrm{ERROR},\mathrm{SAFE},\mathrm{UNCERTAIN}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. We define <em id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">broad mitigation</em> as a baseline ERROR changed to either SAFE or UNCERTAIN, <em id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">strict repair</em> as ERROR <math id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> SAFE, and <em id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">safe regression</em> as a baseline SAFE changed to a non-SAFE outcome. “Overall” reports these transitions over the corresponding baseline population in the complete test set, whereas “Activated” additionally conditions on trajectories where at least one sGDS episode is opened. We compare two intervention configurations. The full intervention uses <math id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=50</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math> until release, whereas the bounded configuration uses <math id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=100</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=3</annotation></semantics></math>, and a maximum intervention window of <math id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=64</annotation></semantics></math> tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ 5.4.1 Admission Selectivity and Timing ‣ 5.4 Evaluation ‣ 5 SingProbe-Med: On-Demand Medical-Risk Intervention ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> reports the paired correction results. The full intervention mitigates 25.03% of baseline erroneous generations over the complete test set, including 12.58% that are strictly repaired from ERROR to SAFE. On trajectories where intervention is actually activated, broad mitigation and strict repair increase to 30.27% and 15.22%, respectively, indicating that the admission mechanism concentrates intervention on trajectories with greater correction potential. Restricting intervention to a 64-token window preserves most of this benefit. The bounded configuration achieves 24.30% broad mitigation and 11.72% strict repair overall, retaining 97.1% and 93.2% of the corresponding full-intervention results. This suggests that most useful corrections occur in the early suffix following activation rather than requiring persistent dual-branch decoding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Intervention nevertheless introduces a non-zero risk of modifying originally safe generations. Reported safe regression is 1.84% overall for the full intervention and 2.53% for the 64-token configuration, with higher rates when conditioning specifically on activated trajectories. This trade-off further motivates selective admission rather than applying sGDS indiscriminately.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.4.3 </span>General Capability Preservation</h4>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next examine whether selective intervention perturbs model capability on inputs for which medical-risk steering is unnecessary. We compare native AntAngelMed-100B, always-on sGDS, and SingProbe-Med across AIME24/25 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maxwell-Jia, 2024</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang and Math-AI Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, HealthBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arora et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, CFBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Arena-Hard-v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, AlignBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and WritingBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Evaluation follows each benchmark’s native scoring convention: AIME24/25 averages the 2024 and 2025 scores, CFBench reports CSR/ISR/PSR, and the remaining benchmarks retain their native scales. For intervention-based methods, the activation rate is defined as the percentage of benchmark examples that open at least one sGDS episode.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ 5.4.3 General Capability Preservation ‣ 5.4 Evaluation ‣ 5 SingProbe-Med: On-Demand Medical-Risk Intervention ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>, SingProbe-Med activates on only 4.69% of HealthBench examples and on none of the reported examples from AIME24/25, CFBench, Arena-Hard-v2, AlignBench, or WritingBench. Its capability scores remain broadly comparable to native AntAngelMed-100B across these evaluations. In contrast, always-on sGDS modifies every example and records lower scores than SingProbe-Med on all six benchmarks, with particularly noticeable degradation on AIME24/25 and Arena-Hard-v2.</p>
</div>

<tr id="S5.T15.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T15.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row">AntAngelMed-100B <math id="S5.T15.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>+</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+</annotation></semantics></math> SingProbe signals</th>
<td id="S5.T15.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right"><math id="S5.T15.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>37.379</td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T15.2.4" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T15.2.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row">Full resident dual branch</th>
<td id="S5.T15.2.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right">60.934</td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T15.2.5" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T15.2.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb">64-token on-demand window</th>
<td id="S5.T15.2.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb"><math id="S5.T15.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>39.162</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.4.4 </span>Inference Efficiency</h4>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we evaluate whether on-demand intervention reduces the inference cost of dual-branch decoding. We compare four AntAngelMed-100B inference configurations: native single-branch decoding, single-branch decoding with continuous SingProbe-Med monitoring, a fully resident dual-branch configuration, and a bounded 64-token intervention window. The single-branch and resident dual-branch entries are reference measurements. The target-plus-SingProbe-Med and 64-token entries are component-based estimates derived from the measured single-branch latency and the corresponding additional signal or active-window cost, and are therefore marked with <math id="S5.SS4.SSS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math> in Table <a href="#S5.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ 5.4.3 General Capability Preservation ‣ 5.4 Evaluation ‣ 5 SingProbe-Med: On-Demand Medical-Risk Intervention ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Continuous SingProbe-Med scoring contributes an estimated 0.060 seconds beyond the 37.319-second single-branch reference, yielding approximately 37.379 seconds before intervention cost is considered. Maintaining the full dual branch throughout generation increases the request-level mean latency to 60.934 seconds, an additional 23.615 seconds over native decoding. In comparison, a 64-token intervention window introduces an estimated 1.843-second active-window cost, giving approximately 39.162 seconds when added to the single-branch reference. These results show that bounding sGDS to the admitted suffix converts persistent dual-branch computation into a limited intervention cost. Together with the correction results above, they demonstrate that most of the safety benefit of full intervention can be retained without continuously executing the second branch throughout generation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduced SingProbe, an intrinsic guardrail that directly leverages hidden states produced by the base LLM to jointly monitor query intent, response safety, and hallucination risk throughout generation. By reusing representations already computed during decoding, SingProbe avoids redundant text encoding and enables fine-grained streaming detection with substantially lower deployment complexity than standalone guardrail models. We also introduced SingStreamBench to evaluate the temporal behavior of streaming safety detectors, particularly their ability to remain silent on benign prefixes and identify the onset of unsafe content. Across extensive offline and online evaluations, SingProbe achieves strong performance on safety and hallucination detection while maintaining very low false-positive rates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">More importantly, our results suggest that the value of intrinsic guardrails extends beyond passive classification. SingProbe scores contain information about the safety tendency of future continuations and can therefore serve as control signals for constrained decoding. SingProbe-Med further demonstrates how such internal-state signals can support selective, on-demand intervention in a high-stakes domain, modifying generation only when and where intervention is warranted. Overall, SingProbe provides a lightweight interface between the internal representations of an LLM and generation-time safety mechanisms, offering a path toward guardrails that jointly improve monitoring granularity, computational efficiency, and actionable runtime control.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="Ax1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix">Appendix</h2>

</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Adaptation to More Open-Source Base Models</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We extend the availability of SingProbe by adapting SingProbe to a broad set of mainstream open-source base models. The adapted models include the Qwen3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Qwen3.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026a</a>)</cite>, Qwen3.6 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026b</a>, <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026c</a>)</cite>, and Qwen3.8 series; the Llama 3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori et al., 2024</a>)</cite> series; the Gemma 4 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2026</a>)</cite> series; the Ling 3.0 series; the gpt-oss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agarwal et al., 2025</a>)</cite> series; the GLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., 2026</a>)</cite> series; and representative models from the StepFun <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">StepFun Team, 2026</a>)</cite>, MiniMax <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen and others, 2026</a>)</cite>, DeepSeek <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and Hy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tencent Hy Team, 2026</a>)</cite> families. This effort makes the same SingProbe interface available across commonly used model families, parameter scales, and architectures.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A1.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ Appendix A Adaptation to More Open-Source Base Models ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> lists the adapted base models and their corresponding SingProbe repositories. Each probe is intended for use with the paired base-model repository shown in the table.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T16" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 16: </span>SingProbe adaptation and release coverage across open-source base models. Base Model and Probe Model report Hugging Face repository IDs.</figcaption>
<div id="A1.T16.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:327.8pt;height:215.9pt;vertical-align:-106.5pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-110.3pt,72.7pt) scale(0.597726184654851,0.597726184654851) ;">
<table id="A1.T16.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="A1.T16.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T16.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.5pt 4.2pt;"><span id="A1.T16.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Base Model</span></th>
<th id="A1.T16.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.5pt 4.2pt;"><span id="A1.T16.2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Probe Model</span></th>
<th id="A1.T16.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.5pt 4.2pt;"><span id="A1.T16.2.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Base params</span></th>
<th id="A1.T16.2.1.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.5pt 4.2pt;"><span id="A1.T16.2.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Probe params</span></th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Evaluation of Adapted SingProbe Models</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the adapted probes with the same benchmark suites used in the main text. Table <a href="#A2.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Appendix B Evaluation of Adapted SingProbe Models ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> summarizes the headline metrics, followed by detailed results for query classification, response safety, and response hallucination.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Across the adapted releases, query F1 ranges from 0.8334 to 0.8811, response-safety F1 from 0.8334 to 0.8729, response-level streaming AUC from 0.9740 to 0.9905, and token-level streaming AUC from 0.9175 to 0.9508. The pooled benign false-positive rate remains at or below 0.08% for 27 of the 29 models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T17" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 17: </span>Evaluation summary for the adapted SingProbe models. Query F1 and response-safety F1 are macro averages over six and eight benchmarks, respectively. Streaming metrics are averages over three benchmarks. Benign FPR is pooled over five benign datasets (lower is better), and hallucination AUC is the macro average over six benchmarks.</figcaption>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Query Intent Classification</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T18" title="Table 18 ‣ B.1 Query Intent Classification ‣ Appendix B Evaluation of Adapted SingProbe Models ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a> reports query-intent F1 for every benchmark. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-singprobe achieves the highest macro F1 (0.8811), while Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-singprobe, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-singprobe, and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-singprobe also exceed 0.8750. Results do not increase monotonically with parameter count: several compact models remain competitive, including Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-singprobe (0.8640) and Qwen3.5-4B-singprobe (0.8650). The OpenAI Moderation split is generally the most challenging, whereas XSTest and HarmBench yield consistently high F1.</p>
</div>

<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Response Safety Evaluation</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Response-level Classification.</span>
Table <a href="#A2.T19" title="Table 19 ‣ B.2 Response Safety Evaluation ‣ Appendix B Evaluation of Adapted SingProbe Models ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a> gives the response-unsafety F1 results. Qwen3.5-27B-singprobe obtains the highest macro F1 (0.8729), closely followed by Ling-3.0-flash-singprobe (0.8728). The narrow spread among many models—especially those above 4B parameters—indicates that the lightweight probe extracts a consistent response-safety signal across base-model families. No single base model dominates every dataset, which also highlights the importance of evaluating across heterogeneous safety distributions.</p>
</div>

<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Streaming Safety Detection.</span>
Table <a href="#A2.T20" title="Table 20 ‣ B.2 Response Safety Evaluation ‣ Appendix B Evaluation of Adapted SingProbe Models ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a> reports response-level and token-level streaming AUC in the same format as the main-text streaming evaluation. Response-level discrimination is uniformly strong, with every model reaching at least 0.9740 mean AUC. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-singprobe gives the highest mean response-level AUC (0.9905). For the more demanding token-localization metric, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-singprobe performs best (0.9508), followed by Hy3-singprobe (0.9498), Qwen3-8B-singprobe (0.9484), MiniMax-M2.7-singprobe (0.9483), and Ling-3.0-flash-singprobe (0.9481).</p>

<div id="A2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">False Positives on Benign Responses.</span>
Table <a href="#A2.T21" title="Table 21 ‣ B.2 Response Safety Evaluation ‣ Appendix B Evaluation of Adapted SingProbe Models ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a> reports false-positive rates on benign model generations. False positives are rare for nearly all probes and are concentrated in Dolly-15k. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-singprobe has the lowest pooled FPR (0.01%); Qwen3.6-27B-singprobe and Hy3-singprobe follow at 0.02%.</p>

<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Response Hallucination Evaluation</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T22" title="Table 22 ‣ B.3 Response Hallucination Evaluation ‣ Appendix B Evaluation of Adapted SingProbe Models ‣ SingProbe Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a> reports hallucination-detection AUC. GLM-5.3-singprobe attains the highest displayed macro AUC (0.8170), followed by GLM-5.2-singprobe (0.8118), Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-singprobe and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-singprobe (both 0.8117), and Qwen3.6-27B-singprobe (0.8094). FaithDial yields consistently high AUC, while FAVA is generally the most challenging benchmark.</p>
</div>
